kirtipasha-zamindar-bari.desc: The Kirtipasha zamindar house was once the seat of a powerful family in the area. Today its mansions and halls stand in ruins, with crumbling walls and arched openings still impressive in scale. Ponds and old temples are scattered around. It sits on the route to Bhimruli, so the two make a natural pair.
blocks: Auto from Jhalokathi town towards Kirtipasha.

khanbari-mosque-complex.desc: In East Angaria village, about 2.5 km from Rajapur, three mosques stand in a row from south to north, built to the same design but in rising sizes. Local history says Kishor Khan, whose family came from Afghanistan to preach, built them in the first half of the 18th century, and they are known as Allah, Muhammad and Fatema. Each has one dome and four octagonal corner towers. Only the largest is still used for prayers, and it holds just 21 people. Kishor Khan's tomb lies to the south and an old pond with a ghat to the east. The complex was declared a protected monument in 2005.
blocks: From Jhalokathi town take a bus or auto to Rajapur, then a rickshaw or auto about 2.5 km to East Angaria.
The active mosque is tiny, so step in only outside prayer times and dress modestly. Ask locals for 'Khanbari masjid'.

gabkhan-bridge.desc: The Gabkhan Bridge carries the Barishal–Khulna highway over the Gabkhan channel, an important inland waterway. From the top, cargo vessels and small boats look tiny on the water. Locals gather here in the evening for the breeze and sunset. It is a quick but scenic stop for travellers passing through.
blocks: On the highway near Jhalokathi town; reachable by auto.
Watch out for traffic on the bridge; use the footpath.

glance: 200 km to Jhalokathi by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
chhoilar-char.desc: Chhoilar Char rose out of the Bishkhali river at Kathalia a little over a decade ago and now covers about 70 acres. It takes its name from the tens of thousands of chhoila trees that grew up on it, mixed with keya, hogla and other plants. Mynas, waterhens and herons are common. The district administration listed it as a tourist spot in 2015, but it has never been developed: there is no jetty, no toilets and no paths, and visitors wade through mud to get ashore. For those who like rough edges, it is one of the least-known green spots in the south.
blocks: From Jhalokathi go by road to Kathalia, then hire a boat from Kathalia launch ghat; there is no road access.
Go between January and March when the char is dry. Wear clothes and sandals you can get muddy, carry water, and go with a local boatman; return before dark.

jhalokathi-amra.desc: Jhalokathi and Pirojpur share Bangladesh's main amra belt, and orchards here line the same canals as the guava trees. The fruit is crisp, sour and slightly fibrous. It is eaten raw with spices, pickled, or made into chutney. In season, boats carry amra to the floating markets alongside guava.

glance: Approx. 20–50 BDT per kg in season
jhalokathi-guava.desc: Guava is the pride of Jhalokathi, and the orchards around Bhimruli and Kirtipasha produce huge quantities in the monsoon. The fruit is crisp and refreshing, eaten fresh or sliced with salt and chilli. In peak season it is very cheap at the floating markets. Vendors across the country sell 'Barishal guava' from this belt.

glance: Nagen Ghosh at Sadhanar Mor, Gopal Ghosh at Bara Bazar and Debnath Mistanna Bhandar at Kamarpatti, Jhalokathi town
jhalokathi-rasgolla.desc: Jhalokathi town has made rasgolla for over a hundred years. Sweet makers boil fresh cow's milk over wood fires, split it into chhana, roll it into balls and simmer them in sugar syrup until they are soft and full of juice. Each piece is a generous 70–80 grams. Old shops around Sadhanar Mor, Bara Bazar and Kamarpatti still draw buyers from all over the country.

glance: 200 km to Jhalokathi by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
bhimruli-floating-market.desc: Bhimruli, on the Kirtipasha canal, hosts the largest of the region's floating guava markets. In season, hundreds of canoes piled with green fruit gather, and traders move from boat to boat to bargain. Surrounding canals pass guava and amra orchards, with small bridges and homesteads along the banks. Hiring a boat to explore the waterways is the best way to see it.
blocks: From Jhalokathi town take an auto to Bhimruli (about 30 min), or come from Barishal by road.
Go early on a market morning in July or August; carry a dry bag and wear sandals.

jhalokathi-shitalpati.desc: Shitalpati, literally 'cool mat', is woven from thin strips of the murta plant, split and sometimes dyed. The finished mat is smooth and stays cool to sit or sleep on in the hot months. Jhalokathi's weavers, many of them women, make plain and patterned mats. The district's motto names shitalpati alongside guava, showing its place in local pride.
blocks: Ask in Jhalokathi town for weaving households and buy directly from makers.

glance: 200 km to Jhalokathi by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
saturia-zamindar-bari.desc: Sher-e-Bangla A. K. Fazlul Huq was born on 26 October 1873 at the Mia Bari of Saturia, his mother's family home, and spent his early childhood here studying at the maktab inside the compound. The estate was founded by his maternal grandfather Ali Mia and once spread over a large area of ponds, gardens and Mughal-style buildings. Today only ruins of the old buildings remain, and most of his belongings have been lost. The site was declared protected in 2010, and a Sher-e-Bangla memorial library has been set up nearby. Descendants of the family still look after the grounds.
blocks: From Jhalokathi town go by bus or auto to Rajapur, then a local auto to Saturia village.
Little is left of the original buildings, so come for the history rather than the architecture. Pair it with the Khanbari mosques near Rajapur.

glance: 200 km to Jhalokathi by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
sugandha-riverfront.desc: Jhalokathi grew as a river port, and its ghats on the Sugandha still see launches, cargo boats and fishermen. Old warehouses and narrow lanes near the river hint at its trading past. Evenings here are calm, with boats passing in the fading light. Few travellers stop to look.
blocks: Walk from Jhalokathi town centre to the launch ghat.
Late afternoon is best; take care on slippery steps.
